utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Beqiraj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies today. Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Beqiraj.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, we talked about the rights of the Albanian population being violated when education was concerned. Given that you were quite active in that respect since you worked in education, I will have a few additional questions concerning the period involved, as well as some relatively recent events. I'm interested in the following: Do you know of the agreed measures to implement the agreement on education from the 1st of September, 1996, and do you know of the agreement at all that was reached by the then president, Slobodan Milosevic, and Dr. Ibrahim Rugova as a representative of the Albanian population?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know of that event, but to my knowledge this agreement failed. If I'm not mistaken, in 1997 and even earlier, students staged protests which were violently suppressed by the police. The students were beaten, prosecuted, and everything ended badly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall why such protests were launched, the protest of students and Albanians in general in 1996, and what seemed to be the main cause of it?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember fully why, but these protests were launched because they asked for freedom, democracy, and for the freeing of the school facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The 1997 demonstrations, did they put forth as their main objective the independence of Kosovo, or did they have indeed a purely educational agenda?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were also for independence, if I'm not mistaken, but I cannot give you explicit reasons because a long time has passed and I wasn't involved in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Given that you knew of the agreement between Dr. Rugova, the late Rugova, and the then president, now deceased, Mr. Milosevic, do you know of the measures that were to be put in place in order to implement the agreement of the 1st of September, 1996. The measures carry a date in 1997. Sorry, March 1998.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollections of these measures. The only thing I know is, however, that this agreement failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What followed, historically speaking, was the opening of the Institute for Albanian Studies in Pristina on the 31st of March, 1998. It was handed over completely to Albanian professors and students. Given that you are a teacher of the Albanian language and that the Institute for Albanian Studies meant a whole lot to your population, do you know what took place at the institute on the 31st of March and before that, on the 23rd of March, 1998? I don't know whether you will agree with me if I say that the agreement was signed by Fehmi Agani, Abdyl Ramaji, Rexhep Osmani, Ratomir Vitco, Goran Percevic, Djobrosav Bjeletic, and in attendance was also a member of the Sant'Egidio community, Monsignor Vicenzo Paglia. Do you know agree with me concerning these facts?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I am not aware who took part in this agreement. If I'm not mistaken, however, this institute of Albanological studies. As I said yesterday, a few facilities were vacated for Albanians to use them, but they were handed over to Albanians in a very poor state. They were destroyed, damaged, and this applies both to the physical facilities and to the books, the equipment in the possession of the institute. In my opinion, this was a tactic in order to beguile the international community that they were allegedly giving the Albanians their rights, whereas in fact the university facilities were completely banned for Albanians, and this is a fact of life, because we were obliged to work in private facilities, in make-shift schools. We had to sit on the floor and to take lectures in these conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why those facilities were in poor condition?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which facilities?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I have in mind those you refer to, the school buildings, faculty buildings.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that when the institute was given over to the Albanians, it was in a very poor state. I didn't see it myself, but I heard it from others that it was in such a wretched condition. In the facilities, make-shift facilities, I worked in, the situation was, as I said, very, very difficult, but we had the will to continue. That's why we managed to survive in those very hard conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many faculties or schools there were under the umbrella of Pristina University?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were many, but I don't know how to describe them. I don't know all of them. Maybe the education officials would be in a better position to give you an idea, the deans, the rectors who are involved in such a work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that by virtue of this agreement there were eight university facilities given to Albanian students for use? In physical terms that included seven buildings covering some 30 different schools, and they also received the keys to the student restaurant, dorms, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about that. The only thing I know is that the students were taught in private homes. This is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of the return of Albanian students to higher educational facilities?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge of that. Until 1998, I was a student and was taught in those private facilities, until the end of 1998, and I didn't see any changes. Personally, I didn't set foot in the faculty of philological studies of which I was a student. I have no information about other universities, but my colleagues said that they, too, were being taught in private homes. They studied there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beqiraj, back in 1996, 1997, and 1998, the late Mr. Rugova, was he a legitimate representative of the Albanian community? What about Fehmi Agani, Abdul Rrahman, and Rexhep Osmani? Were they also representatives of the Albanian population at the time given that those people were involved in negotiations with the then Serbian President, late Mr. Milosevic? In your knowledge and opinion were they legitimate representatives of the Albanian population?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were legitimate representatives of the Albanian people since they were elected by the people and voted by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Given that they signed the agreement in the presence of the representatives -- well, I will not say a representative of the international community but, rather, a representative of an organisation called Sant'Egidio, and given that they were handed over the buildings, albeit in poor shape, I wanted to ask you this: Did anyone begin attending lectures as of the moment of the conclusion of the agreement, and do you know whether in 1998 the Institute for Albanian Studies was operational at all? When I ask you this, I have in mind to ask you whether there were any professors teaching there and any students attending lectures. Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, with respect to the agreement, I may say that many agreements have been concluded then, but how successful they were, how much they were enforced, this is another issue. It is easy to conclude an agreement, but the problem is to enforce them. That's why I'm saying that these agreements were not properly enforced. As far as the Albanological institute is concerned, I have no information that the professors worked there, because the situation was an unusual one, especially in 1998 it was a situation of war. So I have no information about what you are putting to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My question concerning this situation is the following: Do you know that on the 6th of August, 1998, the Ministry of Education, at a meeting with the representatives of -- the international community and Mr. Kamerun as well as Mr. Djamjanovic who was there on behalf of the Ministry of Education whereupon they concluded an agreement on the funds to be used to renew the three buildings of the technological faculty as well as the student dorm building number 3 in the student settlement, as well as reconstruction of the student dorm building number 3 at the location in the existing student settlement, as well as reconstruction of the old building of the old -- of the old technical faculty, then reconstruction of the amphitheatre building at the location of the old technical faculty, reconstruction and repair of the administrative building of the old technical faculty. It all encompassed a total area of over 12.000 square metres. The price envisaged per square metre at the time was around 450 ecu, which should have been over 400 million ecu in total. These were supposed to be the funds of the Republic of Serbian and its ministry. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about what you're saying, and I don't believe that this is the case. I know that there were a lot of destructions and not reconstructions of building. I heard that churches were built in various sites, churches where no -- where didn't exist there before, and proof of this you can find even today in the university grounds, but as I said, I did not hear that any faculty was reconstructed. I only heard that they were demolished, literature was burned and disappeared, and all these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: A short while ago I asked you whether you knew how it came about that those buildings were destroyed or damaged in Pristina. Do you know who damaged them?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know for sure, but I think that who could have demolished them or destroyed them other than those who work there, who had them in their possession. Until that time, the Serb professors, the Serb students were the ones who owned, let's say, these facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that a person using a certain facility has no interest in destroying it, damaging it? Excuse me. Would you agree with me that the damage caused occurred before 1998?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not -- I don't think so. They were damaged deliberately, and also deliberately hundreds of books were destroyed from these premises. I believe that there are evidence to this. This evidence to the destruction inflicted on these universities. It was a time not for the construction. It was a time for destruction which went on for a decade, a decade of repressions, pressure during which the Albanian people had suffered a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you say yesterday that the Serb population in Kosovo amounted to 5 per cent?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I know from my readings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you mind sharing the source of this information with you? Were their any censuses five or ten years back in Kosovo in which Albanian population also participated?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information of any census taken, but during the voting and on other occasions they have come up with this figure. We have had very good relations with the Serb population until prior to the 1990s, but after what happened, promoting Serb nationalism, hatred was instilled among the two peoples and we came to what we all know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that the answer you gave means that you arrived at an approximate figure of the Kosovo population based on the elections, as you've just explained. If you wish to retract from that, you should do it now.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot retract that because there are data to prove what I'm saying, data which are even internationally recognised, that is, about 92 per cent of the population is Albanian, and about 5 per cent are Serbs, and 3 per cent by other nationalities which live in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The latest of my questions was put because since you have those figures based on the elections, it would mean that members of the Serb population also participated in those elections in addition to the 3 per cent of other ethnicities in Kosovo. I guess you're trying to tell us all that in those elections also the Serbs participated as well as other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Serbs did not participate in elections. They boycotted them. I have no information that the Serbs participated in the election, but it's not the election alone. After 1999, when we returned to Kosova, after the ethnic cleansing and the torture and genocide we were subjected to, if I'm not mistaken, until in 2000, 2001, people began to be supplied with ID cards and to be registered. And this -- from this registration they came up with this figure about the Albanian population, because at that time we received our identity cards, the UNMIK passports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beqiraj, Nis is a town in Central Serbia. It has its own university. I am waiting for documents that will be provided by my legal assistant on the basis of which it can be seen that in 1996, 1997, and 1998 the Nis University planned to enroll 2.400 students. The Pristina University planned to enroll 2.430 students in total. Are you trying to say that or to explain that among the 2.400 students there was a need, of course, and funds were provided from the Serbian budget for that, that 2 -- out of 2.400 persons the population of Serbs would be that 5 per cent and that number of 2.430 in Pristina would correspond to the same number of students in Nis, which is a much larger town in Central Serbia? Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment on that. What I know and I'm sure of is that the number of students in Prishtina was not 2.430. There were far more students, although the situation was as it was at the time and the conditions were poor. The youth did whatever they could to continue their education without any support from the Serb government. On the contrary, the Serbs were being arrested -- correction, the students were being arrested, tortured during the protests. They staged protests in which they raised their voices for democracy, for rights to education without any racial, religious, or national discrimination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I would agree with you, but the only point on which I would disagree with you is that the students did not object to the system of education but because they were in favour of the independence of Kosovo after the constitutional changes which took place in Serbia. Would you agree with me that -- again I'm asking you that the demonstration's main purpose was the independence of Kosovo, and always, always as the motto the Republic of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already mentioned this, that whenever the students demonstrated, they asked for their education facilities, for their rights to education as all the peoples in the world without leaving aside the purpose of being free and able to live freely in your country without being persecuted, tortured, or arrested. These demonstrations were suppressed by the authorities and there are facts that corroborate this. This is all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I am going to agree with you, and at the time it was quite normal for the authorities to react in relation to their citizens regardless of what ethnicity they were, but if the demonstrations were against the constitutional system of a sovereign state at the time, then that applies all the more so. I'm going to complete this part and this topic regarding education because I wanted to check how much you actually know and how well you are informed about that. My last question is: Are you talking at the time -- do you speak a language which at the time was called the Serbo-Croatian and then later was called the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to speak it better before, to write it better and understand it better. However, now I can understand it, but I find it more difficult to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, was bilingual usage guaranteed under the constitution at the time, and what was the official language at the time in Kosovo, including all the official institutions and educational institutions?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The official language at the time was Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Including educational institutions?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the Albanian educational institutions?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: At that point -- actually, now we are talking about the legally existing institutions within the system of a state which at that point in time was called Serbia and its autonomous province which at that point in time was called Kosovo and Metohija. So I'm asking you about those institutions, because the system of that state at that time did not recognise parallel systems. So what was the official language in use? Was it Serbo-Croatian, Serbian, or Serbian and Albanian? This is what I'm asking you. And were there any other languages officially used in Kosovo at that time in keeping with the constitution? If you know.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I please get the time period that the counsel is referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have put from my memory, 1996 to 1998 with a question mark, because like you, I was not sure. But is that the correct period, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour, that's the period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. That will help the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. This is a time of discrimination, and at this time the official language as Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that according to the constitution of the Republic of Serbia the official language in Kosovo and Metohija and in use was also the Albanian?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Prior to 1989, Albanian was also an official language. However, when the constitution of 1974 was violently revoked, the Albanian language was no longer an official language. At this time, we were being stripped of all our rights that other peoples enjoyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beqiraj, you travelled throughout Kosovo. It's not a large area. I travelled in Kosovo. When I travel in Kosovo, I always see signs on which it says Urosevac. Above that it says something else. Do you know -- did you know bilingual signage? For example, Ferizaj and then underneath that Urosevac. This was something that was in force in 1990s, in 1996, 1998. Did you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel repeat the last part of what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- honourable counsel, but the official language, the officiality of a language is measured by whether it is used in institutions, not on road signs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When did you get married, Mr. Beqiraj, in which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: 1994? Do you have a certificate of marriage, the original one from the municipality where the marriage was performed?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And marriage certificate, is that in the Serbian or the Albanian language, or is it only in Serbian or only in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. However, the area where I registered my marriage was inhabited by Albanian majority, and I did notice that the registration -- the registry was recorded both in Albanian and in Serbian. In my opinion, this is not that relevant. What is relevant is the use of the Albanian language in different institutions, be they education or other institutions in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beqiraj, did you ever try to enter into employment as a teacher in the school system which was recognised by the then-sovereign state of Serbia, in the territory which at the time was called the Autonomous Province of Kosovo? Did you take part in any job vacancies to get a job in the Kosovo education system, you yourself?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I enrolled secondary school and higher education at the time. I wasn't looking for a job. I wanted to continue my studies so that -- to provide myself with a better future. When I began my studies, the violent measures were in place. We were forced out from the facilities to the roads, and we had to find a way out from this situation, to find the way how to continue with our education in private houses and facilities so that our youth could continue its education and not remain illiterate. We know, all of us, very well about the situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am now going to move to the events that you cover in your statements of the 14th of April, 1999, in Tirana, that you provided, and this later one that you recognise as the statement that you later read and signed and that was shown to you. You say that there were refugees at your home whom you knew earlier from the village of Opterusa. Do you know where that village is, in which municipality?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, I didn't know this family. I came to know them when they were looking for shelter. There were some facilities that could be given to them. Not in excellent conditions, but they were given to them. This village, to answer your question, is in Rahovec municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When did they come to Prizren precisely where you were and when they took those buildings or facilities which you say were not really all that good. When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, they came there after August 1998. They were staying in some other houses in Prizren. I don't know the reasons why they left their houses in Prizren, the houses that were given to them. They came and knocked at my door, asked for shelter, and we helped them. This is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that in the period that you're talking about, 1998, the town of Orahovac was occupied by the Kosovo Liberation Army members and that the Kosovo Liberation Army for a while that year was completely in control there?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the war I learned that the KLA did have this town under its control for brief period, and subsequently the Serb forces drove them out. There was fighting in Rahovec. Many civilians were killed as a result of these fightings in Rahovec municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In one of your statements you say that one evening 12 young men came to your house because they believed your house to be safer. Safer than what, or safer than who's house? What did those 12 young men mean by that?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. My house was not safer. That's not what I said. I didn't say that my house was safer. There was -- there weren't any safe houses in Kosovo at the time. If I've put this this way, what I meant was the following: These neighbours came there so that we could all together live by those difficult times. This is what I meant by what I said. Nobody was safe and secure at the time. Even if this house was a castle, nobody would have felt safe in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show the statement of the 14th of April, 1999, on the screen. This is Exhibit D003-0395. Can we look at page 2 of the statement, please. And in Albanian as well. This is in B/C/S. Earlier we were looking at the text in Albanian. Now we see the text in B/C/S -- or we actually only had the first page. Your Honours, if you permit me, I would like to read a part to the witness, because you see that paragraph in front of you in English. This is something that I wish to put questions to the witness about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There you have it now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 3 of this statement you say that you decided to place your family in a safer place. You were taking them to an uncle, children, some cousins, in the centre of Prizren, and you stayed in your house with this refugee family. You're probably thinking about this family from Opterusa. Already in the next paragraph you say: "The next evening, 12 young men came to my house to stay with me because they were considering my house safer. They stayed only one night in my house." In reference to this part, I wanted to ask you first if this is what you actually say. If you did not, can you please then explain what actually all this is about so that we can eliminate any dilemmas about this particular point. Your family, I agree -- you took your family to a place that you believed was safer, but these 12 young men thought that your house was safer. Who are they? They spent one night there. Why did they come to your house, and what was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will explain it to you. I did not read or sign the statement. I removed the children and the women to the centre of the town for security reasons. We men remained in the house. Other families in the neighbourhood did the same thing. Some youth and some elderly men had remained in their houses to guard their houses, to look after them. As the situation was such, we decided to stay all together. My house was not a fortification, was not a castle. It was a simple house. So we got together just to be able to live by those difficult times together. It was not for safety reasons. There was no safety in Kosova at the time. Nobody felt safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is clear to all of us. The only thing that I would like to ask you is who are these 12. How was it that they came to you specifically? Who are these 12 young men?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were my neighbours with whom I shared everything. These young men, these neighbours of mine, had also removed their families and sent them to the centre of the town because we heard different stories about horrible things that had happened, police raids, lootings, and so forth. That's why we thought that it would be better for the women and the children to go to the centre. As I mentioned earlier, in the Progres Factory area there were many forces stationed. There were -- there was gunfire continuously. And that's why we decided to do so. I don't know if it was to our best or worst, but this was the decision we took. It was a situation of war. We thought that this would be the best solution for us, and we decided to stay together.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Everything is much clearer now. Can you please tell us, when was the first time that you heard about the Kosovo Liberation Army?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about Kosovo Liberation Army, 1997, when in Drenica three members of the KLA, on the funeral of a teacher from Drenica area that had been killed by the police forces for the first time appeared publicly. Until that time people had little faith that such an army existed. I learned about this after the war. In my opinion, this military organisation was borne out of the people, people that had suffered a lot of repression at the time. These were young men that took weapons in their hands to defend themselves, to defend their families, and to defend their homeland.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beqiraj, did you see how KLA members were armed, what sort of uniforms they wore, and whether they wore any at all?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see them until after the war. After we returned from Albania, I had an occasion to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beqiraj, did you hear of any KLA presence in the environs of Prizren?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of it in Vrini. Outskirts, then Reti [phoen] village of Rahovec municipality and of their presence in other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that members of the KLA killed, tortured, raped both Serb and Albanian population they thought were disloyal to their cause, in their criteria?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge and from what I heard, the KLA abided fully by the laws of war. I remember very well a time when they had kidnapped some prisoners, and they exchanged them with Serb forces. In my opinion, the KLA abided by all the law -- laws of the war. It is an army that was incited as a result of use of force to protect its population, to protect their hearts. You cannot accuse such an army of kidnappings, violations, killing of civilians. It's another thing when we talk of a conflict between the two belligerent sides. It would be the same if in the course of a war things happen, but to commit ethnic cleansing of a civilian population, this is beyond understanding and reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will certainly agree with you, Mr. Beqiraj, in that regard. However, I failed to understand whether you were a witness to or whether you only heard of any exchanges. You said they kidnapped some people and then exchanged them later. What was it all about? What were you trying to tell us?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, they took some prisoners. Whether they were -- war prisoners. Whether they were soldiers or not, I don't know, but I think they were soldiers. They were Serbs. And to my knowledge, they negotiated to exchange the prisoners. I don't know if that took effect, but my point was that the KLA implemented the laws of the war. It was an army with scarce weapons, not professionally organised because it was an army formed in a very difficult situation but which was the outcome of force, repression exerted against our population. Any people in the world would have done the same to protect itself from ethnic cleansing, from being murdered. As to what you are saying about kidnappings or rapes of civilians, this is something that I have no knowledge about. Frankly speaking, I don't know that, and I don't believe in such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you responded by saying that you saw KLA members after the war. What you are testifying to now concerning the exchange seems to have taken place during the war. Could you please explain the contradiction? Who did you learn this from, and how do you know about it? To learn of an exchange is a thing of confidence. Only someone who had contact with the KLA could have known about such prisoners. Could you please explain the whole situation to me?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that through radio and television, to my recollection, because I didn't have any contacts with the KLA because I was simply a teacher and also a student. I told you the truth. I saw KLA uniforms and KLA members only after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification, Mr. Beqiraj. Do you know a person by the name of Resadija Morina from Prizren?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Ulcinjska street is in Prizren, and how far from your house is it?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the crow flies, 500 or so metres, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that on the 6th of February, 1999, it was reported that members of the KLA, on the 4th of February, armed with automatic rifles in Ulcinjska street 105 in Prizren, kidnapped Milaim Morina and his cousin, Zeknja Nedo. Do you have any knowledge of that? It has to do with the name of the person I just mentioned recently in addition to the two persons referred to just now. It is Resadija Morina, the person reporting the event in February 1999, before a NATO bombardment, in Ulcinjska street in Prizren. The other people are Milaim Morina and Zeknja Nedo, both from Prizren?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, I have no idea of such an event.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the name of Senad Bajrami in Prizren?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are familiar with the -- with Kosovska Udorna Brigada street in Prizren, and how far is it from your house?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I am not familiar with it because, as I said, a long time has passed since then and the name of the streets have been changed. So I'm not familiar with that. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know of that street. However, do you have any knowledge of an event that took place on the 8th of March, 1999, around 8.30 in the evening? Some KLA members attacked and seriously injured Morina Maska Zeren. I think that was his last name. Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea about that either. To tell you the truth, many things, many terrible things used to happen at that time. People were killed, tortured, and one cannot keep track of everything that happens, so I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of an event which took place on the next day, the 9th of March, again in the evening, Imer Xhhfiqi was kidnapped, a resident of Prizren. Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge or information, direct or indirect, about the incidents which took place in the environs of Prizren in the area of Mala Krusa, Randubrava, Jablanica, Nova Celle, Zagradska, Hoca, as the incidents caused by the KLA, whereas it was allegedly reported as events caused by the Serb forces? These events I'm referring to seem to have been initiated by KLA members and they occurred in the environs of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please make this question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I referred to certain villages in the environs of Prizren. I will not repeat them for the sake of time, but I will put a general question. Do you have any information about the incidents, violent incidents caused by the KLA in the environs of Prizren in the villages I just referred to?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no information about that. And the KLA did not exert any violence against Albanians or against civilians in general from what I have heard and read.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The statement of the 14th of April, which was not signed and read to the witness, could that be admitted into evidence, either in parts that were presented to him or in total before I call up the next exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That, Your Honours, will be assigned --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: -- [overlapping speakers] D00120.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask for a 65 ter document to be put up. It is the Kosovo album, P615, page 48. That should be a map of Prizren town. Could we enlarge it a bit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While that is happening, could I mention for the transcript that page 22, line 10, the statement of the 14th of April, 1999, was made Exhibit D00120.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Beqiraj, do you see the map in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the usher to assist Mr. Beqiraj and provide him with an electronic pen. Mr. Beqiraj, given that you reside in Prizren, I suppose that the next few questions will not be difficult for you. Could you please put a 1 next to the place where your house was, next to the road Djakovica-Prizren. Could we see the approximate location of your house on this map.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the parts of the town? Does this map enable you to do so? Could you please mark the centre of town for me. Mark it with a circle and put an X in it. Where's the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very unclear here in the map, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Unclear. I see. I don't have another Prizren map, and I don't think we could find another one in the Kosovo atlas.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, I find it hard to find it. I'm afraid I can give you the wrong information, misplace the centre, that's why I hesitate to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you read the names of the parts of the town in white? I don't know whether you can make them out.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My assistant will try to come up with a better map, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the Chamber for the time we're using on this, particularly in view of the fact that I promised to conclude my cross-examination in the course of the first session. We definitely don't have another map. I will press on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Between the 24th and the 28th of March, you and your family went to Prizren and back to your house on several occasions. When I say Prizren, I mean the centre of town, to your uncle. And you also travelled back to your home. In the course of the four days, did you or your family members face any unpleasant situations? Were there any incidents on the way to the uncle's house and back?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we decided to leave together with the family, I explained also yesterday that in the village, that in our neighbourhood there were only four families that had remained. The others had fled out of fear of something terrible happening. Then we, too, decided to leave in the direction of the city to go to some of our relatives living in the centre of the town. While we were walking on the side-streets to enter the centre of the city, we left at about 7.00. When we passed the main road, Prizren-Gjakove main road, we hurried in order not to be detected by the Serb forces, because we were afraid we might fall victim to them. And very soon we passed the road. We entered the side-street to go where we wanted to go. While we were walking along these side-streets, some family members came out of their houses and saw us walking, and we also heard some shots at 8.00 in the evening. We heard that NATO had struck some military barracks. And these people told us, "Don't continue, because you might fall victims." That's why we stopped and spent the night in some house there. We heard various fire -- fires being -- rifles being shot at these houses. The bullets hit the walls of this house, broke some glass. And it was a horrible night for us, but there was no other solution for us. We had to stay that night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I will limit myself only to the most important questions and cut down on the rest of them. As you were moving towards the Albanian border on the tractor trailer, you mentioned some escort and other things, including many of the things contained in the statement given to the OTP. Can you tell us this: On the left and the right-hand side of the road, did you notice that both sides of the road towards Morina were mined? When I say that, I'm not asking whether you saw the mines themselves, but did you see any signs which said "Mines," any markings pointing to the fact that the area had been mined on your way to the Albanian border?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see any such signs. I can recount here very frankly some story I heard from some other people. Because among the forces, the Serb forces, there were some good people. A policeman or a military, I don't know who he was, had advised this person not to walk along on the -- on the side of the street because it was mined. But these -- such people were very few, but I did -- other than that, I didn't see any signs showing that the zone was mined. That's why I'm saying -- frankly speaking, this is what I heard from someone else. When we returned from Albania, I saw that the streets were mined. The asphalt road was destroyed in several places. From Morina to Prizren there were traces showing that the streets -- the area had been mined.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me when I say that there were no visible signs on the -- by the side of the road, that the nearby area on your way to the border was mined? There were no signs.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were holes. It was mined, but there were no signs showing that it is mined. This is what I heard from others, but I also saw these holes myself when I came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because it is unclear to me what the need was to have an escort. If it was general knowledge that there were mines around, no one in their right mind would stray from the street or the road. That is why I was asking you. Before I conclude, I wanted to ask you this: Yesterday you mentioned verbal abuse that you suffered in the hands of the Serbs, and some gestures they made. They said things to the effect, "Where is your KLA now? Where is your NATO and Thaqi now?" At that time, what was the status of Thaqi? How well known may he have been to the Serb forces at the time? There was someone else there who was much more prominent as regards the Albanian population at the time, I believe.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, at that time Thaqi was one of the most prominent figures in the KLA. He was also present in the negotiations. This is from what I saw on television and also after the war when he became more well known. So people knew who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I noticed that your wife's maiden name is Thaqi. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is she Hasim Thaqi's cousin?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, she's not. There are many families in Kosova that bear this last name, but she has got nothing to do with Thaqi's family. In every town or in every village there are families by this last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Beqiraj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will make good on my promise and conclude my cross-examination. I believe it is also the time for the break. There may have been some questions that I believe may have illustrated the situation better, but I tried to cut down my cross-examination. Therefore, I decided not to put them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Gopalan, do you need re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honours. My estimate would be around 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will break now. Could I ask you to confine your cross-examination more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just look at the matters that are important, and the political history is not something that is going to determine any of the issues on this indictment --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you are for your guidance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- I make that clear. Could I also mention for the assistance of all prosecuting counsel that there has been developing a tendency with recent witnesses of tendering a statement and then spending a very long time going through parts of that statement with the witness. We have been losing time unnecessarily with that. There, of course, will be matters that need clarification or amplification in some statements, but there is no value in terms of our proceedings in having a witness just go over again, perhaps only for emphasis, matters that are already dealt with in the statement which is exhibited. The purpose of Rule 92 bis and ter is to shorten proceedings by the use of a written statement in lieu of evidence, not as a further way of giving the same evidence. So we would like all prosecuting counsel to be aware of that. We must have our first break now. For tape and other reasons we need half an hour. We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan, re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I just have a few --

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: -- questions remaining for you today, and this is the first group just in relation to your personal experiences of the education system as a teacher and as a student, and if I could ask you to confine your answers to your own experiences. Now, at page 4823, you were asked about the parallel education system, and you said, "We wanted to enroll in the normal education system, but the police surrounded the premises and did not allow us to enter these premises." Did you experience this yourself, the premises you were in being surrounded by the police?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is true. On the 1st of October, the new academic year was supposed to begin. I had only been admitted -- I had already been admitted to this faculty, and we were denied entry to the high pedagogical school in Prizren. The premises were surrounded by Serb forces. The students' union held a speech in our presence in an effort to make up their mind so as they would be allowed to enter the school premises.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to clarify, sir, when you say the 1st of October, could you tell us which year that was in?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1st of October, 2001, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb forces surrounded us --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Just to clarify, did you just say the 1st of October, 2001?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. 1991. That's a mistake on my part. The students who held that speech were arrested afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you say the high pedagogical school, what level of education was this institute? You refer to a faculty as well. Was this a school? Was this a university? If you could just clarify that for us.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was of a faculty level. It belonged to university of Prishtina. People of different ethnicities used to study in that facility. It's a higher education institution.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Later on in your testimony you speak about being educated in a private home, and you say that you were often -- or "We were often subjected to police assaults, raids. They came and confiscated school materials and so on." Now, these police assaults and raids, again is this something you yourself experienced?

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of some of the raids, and we managed to escape one of the raids thanks to a professor of ours. Just before this raid was carried out, we abandoned the facility. During these raids, professors and students were arrested. Their student booklets were seized. Other materials were seized. We didn't feel safe in the areas where we studied or taught. It happened occasionally that we would try to find safer areas to carry out our studies and teaching.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And when you refer to the facility that you abandoned just prior to the raid, could you clarify, if you remember, when it was that you had to abandon this facility, and if you could also explain what this facility was.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a mosque hall. The mosque allowed us to use this hall for teaching purposes. This happened in 1993, to my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, just moving on to my final topic. These are the events that took place round about the time of the NATO bombing. You were asked some questions by my learned counsel about your movement from Prizren town centre and back to your home between the dates of the 24th to the 28th of March, and you say that you passed along the main road - and this is the Prizren-Gjakove main road - and you hide on in order not to be detected by the Serb forces. And I quote here, you say: "Because we were afraid we might fall victim to them." Now, when you say "we might fall victim to them," could you clarify for us, please, what it is you were afraid of of falling victim to.

utterances.speaker: XHAFER BEQIRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation itself we found ourselves at that time for months, the hatred towards us after the NATO bombing commenced, the Serb forces hated us and started to behave savagely. We heard of people disappearing in mysterious circumstances, people whose fates remained unknown. This is the truth, and that's why we were afraid that we would fall victim to the same things.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Beqiraj. I do not have any further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Gopalan. Mr. Beqiraj, you'll be pleased to know that that concludes the questions for you. The Chamber would like to thank you for coming to The Hague and for the assistance that you have been able to give to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're very welcome, Your Honours. I have a request. I would like to ask a question. I don't expect an answer from any of you, but I would just ask you for permission to ask this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For years, I heard the saying that Kosova was the cradle of Serbia. I always found it difficult to understand how it was possible for the cradle of Serbia to be in Kosova and for the children of Serbia to be raised in Serbia. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Nobody will be attempting to deal with that issue. The court officer will assist you out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to ask the question, Your Honours. I didn't ask for any answers. Thank you very much for this opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Behar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The next witness will be Mr. Hyseni, and I believe he can be brought in just as we change seats here and get ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that is given to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Behar has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could you --

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name and your date of birth for the record.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: My name is Bedri Hyseni. I was born on the 16th of October, 1960.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I understand, sir, that you are a Kosovar Albanian, that you were born in Ferizaj but have lived thereafter in the village of Biba in the Urosevac municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's where I still live.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I understand, sir, that you gave an initial statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 8th of May, 1999, about the events that you experienced in Kosovo and that you provided a second statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 27th of August, 2001, and the 1st of September, 2001; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to read those statements before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I understand that there are a couple of things that you'd like to correct in your statements so that they accurately reflect your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can I have up on the screen 65 ter number 2270, please. And we'll need actually -- it'll be page 3 of your second statement, which will be -- it's page 8 of the PDF file, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: At page 3, this is page 3 of your second statement, at paragraph 3 the first sentence reads: "From 1991 until 1994, I was an activist for the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms." Is that correct or is a change required?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I would like to make a correction. I was an activist with the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms until 1999, from 1991 to 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. On that same page in the English, it's paragraph 5. The second sentence reads: "He was arrested sometime in 1994 or 1995 and sentenced to eight years' imprisonment on charges of terrorism." Is that correct or is a change required there?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: He was arrested in 1993 and spent six years in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And with those changes having been made, are you satisfied that the information that's contained in your statements is true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes. It's accurate to the best of my knowledge and belief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, would I seek to tender those statements and the entire 92 bis package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What do you mean by the entire 92 bis package.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sorry, I just meant to explain that the statements are together in one package under that 65 ter, which is 02270.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The statements will be received as separate exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first one, Your Honours, under -- dated the 8th May, 1999, will be assigned P00808. And the second one with the date 27th of August, 2001, and the 1st of September, 2001 would be assigned P00809.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall testifying at the trial of Milutinovic et al on the 11th of September, 2006?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes. It was on the 11th of September, 2006 that I testified in the trial of Milosevic -- correction, Milutinovic et al.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to review the transcript of your testimony in that trial?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I understand that there are a few clarifications that you'd like to make as well with respect to what was recorded in that transcript. Can I have up 65 ter number 05079. And this will be at page 3092. Sir, at -- at lines 1 to 5 of this page you were asked: "And I understand you're married with three children?" And to this question you answered --

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes. A change is needed here as well. I'm married and I have four children. I apologise for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: That's no problem, sir. Thank you. At page 3109 -- I'll just wait a moment while that's brought up. At lines 10 to 11 the transcript states: "And in February 1999, a collective sentence of 289 months of imprisonment was determined." Is there a clarification that you would like to make there?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes. Not 289 months but 289 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 3112. I'll again just wait a moment while that's brought up. It states at line 13 and 14: "There are two cooperatives there, an agricultural one and one for bees." Is there something you would like to explain or clarify about that?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: It's not a cooperative for bees, but the name of the cooperative is "Bleta," which in English is bees.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And lastly, if we could have up page 3114. At lines 3 to 5 it states: "They bombed the barracks in Ferizaj and some tanks in Komogllave village from the road that goes to Fshati i Vjeter to Postojni." Is there a clarification you would like to make with respect to that?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: There is no locality called Postoni. What I men here was Fshati i Vjeter and Rruga e Shkupit or the Skopje road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And with those clarifications having been made, does the transcript now accurately reflect your evidence and would you testify to those same facts today?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. Can you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I'm just asking that now that we've made those clarifications, does the transcript accurately reflect your evidence, and would you testify to those same facts again today?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it does accurately reflect my evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would seek, please, to tender that transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that, Your Honours, will be assigned P00810.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I would also seek to tender one exhibit that was associated with Mr. Hyseni's testimony, that was 05080, and it is a map from the Kosovo atlas that was marked by the witness when he testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that, Your Honours, will be assigned P00811.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I can now provide a brief summary of Mr. Hyseni's evidence. Mr. Hyseni has a law degree and was a member of the Human Rights Council in Urosevac. He has explained the ongoing persecution of Kosovar Albanians and described how his human rights worker colleagues were imprisoned and even killed for their human rights work on behalf of the Albanian population. He describes that police and police reservists manned check-points on the local roads, that approximately one month prior to NATO bombing the military moved in, and that the military and police armed the Serb civilian populace. Mr. Hyseni describes observations of the actions and deployments of Serb forces beginning with the commencement of the NATO bombing on the 24th of March, 1999 as he moved from his hometown of Biba to Sojevo, and then as he was forced to hide in the mountains along with other Albanian villagers. He describes Serb forces attacking Sojevo burning 90 per cent of the civilian homes and forcing civilians out. He describes travelling in a convoy to Urosevac, being sent back by police to Gnjilan, but instead himself going to Slatina where he remained for 12 days. He will describe the conditions in Slatina where thousands of Kosovar Albanian refugees arrived.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down for the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Fearing what would happen, Mr. Hyseni returned to Urosevac where conditions were terrible. He spent five days there before boarding a bus that was moving Kosovar Albanians across the border to Macedonia. He describes being stopped by VJ and police at a check-point in Kacanik, continuing to the border at Djeneral Jankovic, and making observations of a large police presence there before leaving the country on April 27th and 28th. That is the end of the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, I have some brief questions for you in the time that I have remaining. Picking up somewhat into your -- the account of what happened, after your observations and experiences in Sojevo, you described escaping from Sojevo with your family on the 6th of April and going into the mountains. You described joining about 200 villagers there, and you described in your second statement that this group of people then split into two groups and that your group managed to get away without being noticed, but that this other second group you describe being robbed and forced to walk to Urosevac. My question is can you explain to the Court how it is that you know what happened to this second group?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: This occurred on the 6th of April, that is, during the NATO bombing. A paramilitary and police expedition, supported by the regular VJ soldiers that were deployed at the school building, undertook an operation first in the Limanaj neighbourhood. They killed two persons there, Hamit Halimi and Qerim Havazi and expelled the entire population from that neighbourhood by setting the houses on fire and burning 90 per cent of them. The same group of forces continued and advanced towards my neighbourhood where I was at the time, the neighbourhood of Shukri Begu or Sulaj neighbourhood. There, the paramilitaries and the police burned the houses, killed my uncle on my mother's side, Nazir Nebihu and Hazira Nebihu.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, let me just stop you there for a moment if I can. I know we have -- we have this account from your statement and from your testimony as well. I just wanted to focus, if I could, on the question of these groups, and you described this single group that you were in of about 200 villagers. You described that being divided into two groups, and then you described what happened to that second group. And my specific question for you is: How is it that you knew what happened to the second group?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I thought I was supposed to describe the entire event, but from what I see, you want to know about the other group. I will explain. Initially we were about 200 civilians, elderly people, women, children at the end of the village the group was divided in two parts. One part set out in the direction of Komogllave village in the vicinity of the forest. The other part where my family members were -- were sent to another part, to a forest in a place called Ljubizanis [phoen]. When the paramilitaries set -- set fire to the houses, they saw the other group and were -- went there. We could see from the place we were how they behaved. They were looted, men separated from women and ordered to continue on foot towards Ferizaj, because otherwise they would have been killed by the police. Novica Mijovic was the one who had told the population this. In order to understand the situation better, some of the people from the column tried to flee the column and entered the forest and came back to our group because they were members of some families that were in our group. So they were the ones who told us what happened, how they had been looted, taken away their jewels and every valuable they had on them. That was how I came to learn about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. So just to be clear, sir, then, am I understanding right that there were people from this second group who experienced the things that you described who then rejoined your group afterwards?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: I see. And I see you've mentioned that there were members of some of the same families. So were you personally able to speak to some of these people when they returned to your group as well?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We all talked to them. We are a group of 80 persons, and we talked. I personally talked with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. You explained, sir, that instead of -- well, perhaps I'll put that a different way. You explained staying in Slatina for 10 to 12 days, and you -- you explained in your statement -- you described that there were more than 10.000 people who passed through there in the time that you were there. Can you explain to the Court what the conditions were like in Slatina in those 10 or 12 days that you spent there?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: The conditions in Sllatine were somewhat good, but with the growing number of people coming from Gnjilane, Viti, Ferizaj municipalities, the situation deteriorated, and we started to lack the most elementary things, like foodstuffs and other things. So all this large concentration of population created a humanitarian crisis situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: You described previously that on the 22nd of April of 1999, you travelled to Urosevac, and you explained that you did that to take care of your father-in-law and your brother-in-law and also because you described what you were -- that you were worried about what might happen in Slatina. Can you explain to the Court what it was that you were worried would happen in Slatina?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes. Because of the large concentration of people there, over 10.000 people, there was -- that was the estimate, those who took down numbers and trying to take care of them, the police often came about that area and looted some good cars from the villagers. This was a reason that made me leave the place, because I started fearing for the worst. In fact, it had already started to happen since all that population was driven out and the young people were imprisoned in Viti. I left Sllatine also because my father-in-law and my brother-in-law, on the second night of the air-strikes, if I'm not mistaken, were injured by a shell thrown by the Serb army from the barracks, because their house is situated near the barracks. Since my wife knew nothing of what had happened, I had learned it from the television report, I knew what happened and instead of sending my wife, I thought it would be better, more viable, if I went, and I could provide some assistance to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir. I'd like to ask you a question about Urosevac or Ferizaj, the town, and the time you spent there. You say in your statement that conditions were terrible. Are you able to describe what those conditions were and why you make that characterization?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I made that characterization because in the city neighbourhoods I saw in -- not only in the Lodja area neighbourhood where there were Albanians, but in general circulation was forbidden. In the other -- the other neighbourhoods were free of people because the population had been driven out. In some parts of the town where I could go, because I didn't go all over the town, I saw the presence of the army, the police, paramilitaries, dressed in their specific clothes, long hair, and so on, painted in their faces, but the worst thing was because there was constant shooting and the kids were scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, in your second statement you also describe that on the 27th of April of 1999, you went with a group to the Urosevac bus station where you saw four buses filled with people, and you described boarding one of those buses. Do you know, sir, whether those buses were arranged by Serb forces or by Albanians? Are you able to explain that? If you know.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Of course they were arranged by the Serb forces, because the road to Skopje doesn't -- doesn't employ four or five buses. The bus lines had its own buses once a day, maybe, but that what happened was done deliberately. They wanted to use buses and trains to get rid of the population. I was one who travelled by bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can you explain who was driving those buses?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: The drivers were all Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of the passengers?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: You -- Albanian, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. You described in your statement and in your testimony that your bus was stopped in Kacanik at a check-point. Can you explain who was manning that check-point?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: At the entry to Kacanik there was a check-point and the bus was stopped there. It was manned by a large group of policemen dressed in a strange uniform, a uniform of 1979, 1980, 1981, I would say. They had a light blue ribbon on their army, and there were two reservists, and I knew both. One was a financial inspector. Fisekovic his last name is. The other one sold bread, and he was my generation. He was a baker, but I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Sir, you also described then the bus continuing on to Djeneral Jankovic or Hani i Elezit, and you described that when you arrived there there were numerous policemen there. Can you explain, sir, what those police were doing that you observed?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: These police stood in groups of three mostly, and that long convoy of Albanian refugees that was being driven out was escorted by them along the asphalt road. They stood about 300 to 400 metres far from the column and ordered them to cross the border in groups of ten. So when a family had more than ten, it had to leave two kids behind and then cross it in groups. They gave orders to the refugees what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Can you give us an idea, sir, about roughly how many police you observed there? And was this a large group of police? Was it a small group of police?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: How can I say? They, as I said, were divided in groups of three. Maybe over 30, I suppose. There were a lot of policemen there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And did the police appear to be organised in their actions, in your view?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes, they appeared to be organised. They were dressed in the typical police uniform, dark blue camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: When you were stationed there, sir, when you spent your time there, were you able to hear any orders being issued between police?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I didn't hear any orders being given between them. I wasn't actually interested to hear what was going on among them. The only order I heard was that we had to form groups of ten, not more than ten members, but as to who gave the order, I don't know. It was probably a chain of command giving the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Those are my questions for you, and now my learned friend from the Defence will have some questions for you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Behar. Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I need some time to prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While that's happening, Mr. Behar, there was an amendment to the statement which was Exhibit 809. That was an amendment made, I think, in January 2002. Are you wanting that tendered as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would also seek to tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And that, Your Honours, will be assigned P00812.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Hyseni. My name is Dragoljub Djordjevic. I appear on behalf of the accused in this case. Mr. Hyseni, first of all, I'd like to deal with the misunderstanding. In your brief 65 ter summary that we received in writing from the Prosecutor, the Prosecutor put down that you entered Macedonia on the 27th or the 28th of June, 1999. Do you agree with me that it was actually in April 1999?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: It was in April, yes. It is a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your first statement was provided on the 8th of May, 1999, that is to say -- say while the operation in Kosovo was still under way. Can you tell us how you were contacted by OTP or Tribunal representatives in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: How I was contacted?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: The OTP contacted me because I was in the capacity of the refugee. I was stationed in Stankovac 1, if I'm not mistaken. I met them, and I described the situation to them, the event to them. I gave the first statement. And in order to give such a statement -- I think I had the right to give such a statement in order to give an accurate account of what I'd seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What did you do after 1991? Where did your income come from?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: After 1991, I won my income from a private firm I had. I dealt with production -- I -- actually, I involved in a work as a carpenter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
