utterances.text: You completed your studies at the age of 31 in 1990 or 1991, if I'm not mistaken. You were married in 1986. How did you finance your studies?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I was not married in 1996. I was married in 1986. And it's a fact that I graduated in 1991. There was only one exam left for me. I started in 1985, 1986. 1987 I finish the army in Postojna. But seeing that there were no jobs for Albanians, I -- at that moment I felt I had to interrupt the studies, which I resumed at a later time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You just told us you served your military term in Postojna. What was your military speciality? Which aspect of the army and what were you trained in?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I did my military service in Postojna in Slovenia, in the infantry brigade. I was a shooter, "strelac" in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you try to find work only in the town where you lived, or did you seek employment elsewhere in the territory of the former Socialist Federal Serbian Republic of Yugoslavia as of the moment when you completed your studies?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: When I completed my studies, I did not seek work because the place where I graduated discriminated Albanian employees. Nobody was allowed to work with the exception of those who would recognise Serbia as their own state. I believe you know such things, things that happened in 1989. When Kosova was deprived of its status. So I registered my firm, and I minded my own business as a private entrepreneur.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question was this: Did you try to look for work outside the territory of the Autonomous Province of Kosovo and Metohija to find work as a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you say that there were certain regulations in place which were introduced, as you put it, at the expense of the Kosovo Albanians due to which they could no longer find employment. I would not ask you this question if you were not lawyer, but given that you are, could you tell it us what regulation are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I am referring to well-known regulations introduced in 1991. The factories were closed down to Albanian workers. The police no longer employed Albanian officers who were employed there before. They were dismissed. Even -- if someone wanted to work, if he was working, they had to sign a certain statement which said that Kosova was called Kosova and Metohija and to recognise the Serbian state, which Albanians didn't want to do or refused to do. And all the factories, as I said, and other workplaces were banned for Albanians. They were blocked by police forces who prevented Albanian workers from entering the premises. This is what rules I referred to. These were the rules imposed by Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hyseni, you spoke about this, and we have that in your written statement, but that was not my question, however. Now you are talking about a possible way of behaviour that may have occurred at that time, but I'm asking you as a lawyer. Can you cite a single rule or regulation which would prohibit Albanians from finding work in the territory of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I told you I didn't see any actual act or rule because I was not employed in the state bodies, but the very fact that Albanians reported to work and were dismissed from work, it was -- it must have been based on a rule which Serbia used. I had family members, uncles, cousins, who were employed and whose work relationship was cancelled, exterminated. You know that when somebody's employed, you have to undergo a certain procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: At page 2 of your statement of the 27th of August, 2001, you say that Albanians received a document that they were supposed to sign accepting certain rules of the Republic of Serbia. You said today that it -- it stated that Kosovo was to be called Kosovo and Metohija and some other things. Can you tell us, did you ever see such a document with your own eyes, and, if so, please describe it for us.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I told you I didn't see it myself, because in order to see such a document, a Albanian had to go to his place of work and sign the document in order to go back to work to continue working. But I told you that some of my family members were dismissed from work unless they agreed to -- to sign this document. I suppose I was clear. I said I didn't see it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did any of your relatives, having lost their employment due to not signing such a document, tell you what the document actually said?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: They didn't give me any details, but they only said that the headline said the -- the Serb state and that the Kosova is an autonomous province was called Kosovo and Metohija, which we as Albanians didn't recognise, didn't accept, because Kosova had its own status. It was to its detriment. As it was detrimentally affected by the revocation of its status, by the forceful revocation of its status. You, I believe, remember that this happened with approval of members who were not even members of parliament at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hyseni, we're not so interested in political issues here, and if -- in the extent that you talked about those matters as facts, so I'm not going to go into that, but I just wanted to ask you this: Do you know, and would you agree with me, that the parliament of the autonomous province which existed when the vote was held on the constitution of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija comprised mostly members of the Albanian ethnic group? Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes, it comprised mostly Albanian -- Albanians, but there were also Serbs, but it was called Kosova and not Kosovo-Metohija. It was called Kosova, not Kosovo and Metohija. Then you invented that other syndrome. It has to be eliminated. Kosova has been, is and will remain Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What name is that? Is the word "Dukagjin" an Albanian word or a Serbian word? What does "Dukagjin" mean? How would you be able to say that? Does that mean Metohija?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Dukagjin is an Albanian word. When Serbia uses Metohija, it refers to the religious heritage in Kosova. These churches were defended for centuries by Albanians. It was the Vojvoda family in Decan that defended the church there. The Serbs seem to forget that Albanians belonged to three different religious faiths. To name a country with that religious reference is not right. Kosova's name is Kosova, and it is recognised as such by international conventions and now as an independent state. And it is in conformity with the ruling democracies in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hyseni, do you know what the name of the autonomous province was before 1974?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And Metohija.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: What I know is that it was referred earlier as Kosmet or Kosovo and Metohija just to give rise to Serb nationalism, but that name is not correct. Kosova was always Kosova and still is. That is the adequate name of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We're not going to dwell on this anymore. I would just like to remind you that Metohija is a word of Greek origin. We're not going to discuss this anymore. Can you please tell me, in relation to the Albanian workers in the territory of Kosovo from 1991 until 1999, they were not employed in state factories or in factories, in state bodies and institutions?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: That's correct. They were not employed because they had been previously expelled from work and denied their constitutional right to employment, their freedom to choose their own employment. They were not employed, because they were discriminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Not a single Albanian was employed?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I'm not saying all of them. There were still some who --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We ask not to overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- employed, but this number was small. Those who were loyal to the Serbian policies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When you say a small number, are you aware that in the territory of the municipality of Urosevac, over 700 Albanian employees worked in state institutions alone? Do you know about this information? Seven hundred employees in state institutions. Do you know about this? We're talking about Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: During this period in Ferizaj, more than 700 workers is absolutely not true. Those who were employed in the Serbian state institutions were known. They were small in number. They were not 700. You could count them by the fingers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2, paragraph 5; page 3, paragraph 1 in the English and Albanian, you say that the objective of that was to abolish the status of Kosovo as a federal unit. Was Kosovo ever a federal unit as part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The contusion of 1974 recognises Kosovo as a constitual part of the Yugoslav Federation. It was a federal unit. It was a constituent part. The socialist autonomous province of Kosova was a constituent part of the Yugoslav Federation, and I support this claim by the following fact: The Presidency that was formed after the death of Tito was such that every unit, federal unit, had a mandate of Presidency. When I was a soldier in Postojna in 1987, the president of Yugoslavia was Sinan Hasani who was from Kosova. This fact argues what I just said and what you put to me. It supports the claim that Kosova had had the status of a federal unit. It had its MPs in the federal parliament, and it had its mandate for a president.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And Kosovo was an autonomous province within which state? Was it within the Federal Republic -- Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or the Socialist Federal Republic of Serbia, as it was called at the time?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: It belonged to the Yugoslav Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's what it said?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: It had its own status. It was part of the Yugoslav Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever read in its entirety the constitution of 1974? I must ask you this.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes. It is signed by Ilaz Kurteshi, who was at the time president of the Kosovan Assembly. I did read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And does it say that Kosovo is part of the Socialist Republic of Serbia as an autonomous province within that Republic? Does that state in the constitution? Did you read that or not?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: That's what it states, but we were talking about federal units. Kosovo was a federal unit, and with the constitution of 1974 it had -- it enjoyed equal rights as did the other republics. After the political crisis in Yugoslavia and when it was dissolved as a country, things changed. If we continued to enjoy the same rights as we did before the autonomy was revoked, we wouldn't have had the problems and the disputes we had, and nothing would have happened of what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And as part of your work from 1991 until 1999 when you were in the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms, can you please tell me what were the basic aims of that organisation in which you were an activist? Why? What was the reason it was founded in Kosovo? Was it in order to protect and defend the human rights of all the citizens of Kosovo or because of threatened civil rights of the Albanian ethnic citizens of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: The Council for the Protection of Human Rights and Freedoms was established sometime in 1989, 1990 by a great lawyer, well known in the Balkans, Bajram Kelmendi, then Adem Demaci, Zeni Raguda [phoen], a worker of human rights, Pajazit Nushi, and many other intellectuals. It had its branches in all the municipalities, towns and townlets of Kosova. Its objectives and aim was very clear, to defend the human rights, mainly the rights of those citizens who were subjected to systematic violence exercised by the Serb regime. So our activity was focussed on monitoring these cases of violence that were evidenced in every walk of life in Kosova. The work was such that it demanded meetings to be convened once a week, usually on Saturdays. We would collect information from people who were maltreated in police stations. They would contact us, give us information, although they were threatened by the police not to contact us. But they did. We collected this information, compiled reports, submitted them to the headquarters in Prishtina, and the headquarters in Prishtina would then submit those reports to the Helsinki Committee, so that to inform the international public about what was going on, about the truth prevailing in Kosova at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hyseni. You have saved a few questions with your very detailed and precise answer to my question. Can you please tell me, is there council -- does this council still exist today for the protection of human rights and freedoms in Pristina and in other places?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes. The Council for the Protection of Human Rights still exists in Prishtina. It is led by Dr. Pajazit Nushi. It also exists in other towns but in smaller numbers. There are usually coordinators in these smaller towns, usually two persons that deal with property disputes and other types of disputes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that in 1999, you stopped being active in this council for the protection of human rights. What was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, my activity in the field of human rights never ceased. I still perform this activity. However, in terms of the council and as an activist of that council, I stopped this activity because I was expelled. I became refugee first in Macedonia, then I was moved to Manchester in the UK. That's why I could no longer be an active -- activist of the council. All the work we did at that time during the war was based on our free will. It was voluntary work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And where are you living right now, Mr. Hyseni?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: In Bibaj village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I heard from you today that this council deals more with legal matters today, with resolving property issues and so on, do you have any information that the council today works on the protection of human rights of Serbs who have left Kosovo? Does it deal with matters of protection of their property and of their rights?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: From what I know, somewhere in Sterps [phoen], the Ferizaj branch in Sterps dealt with these issues. There was an employee from Prishtina and another one from Ferizaj, lawyers by profession, who dealt with these issues in the municipalities of Stimlje and Sterps, and I think that these issues were resolved last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The transcript from the Milutinovic case, on page 3093, lines 11 to 13, in response to a question further to you, you replied that -- the question was "If police and military forces of Serbia armed Serbian civilians," you replied, "I didn't see that they were arming them." Can I conclude then that you don't have immediate information about what you said, that Serbian civilians were armed by the army and the police and that that is an assumption of yours and indirect knowledge, but that you don't have any direct knowledge about that, and can you say something else today? Perhaps this is Exhibit P810.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, all civilians, including Serb civilians -- correction, Serb civilians, all of them were armed. There were no Serbs in my village, but in other villages there were, and they were armed. Personally, I didn't see this. I didn't see them being armed, but the information circulating was such that they were being armed. I didn't see the act of issuing weapons with my own eyes, but I know this for a fact because I know the Serb population live -- that lives in the area where I live. Maybe not all of them by name, but by sight I would say I know all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your statement of 1999, on page 3, paragraph 6 of the B/C/S, and paragraph 2, page 3 of the English --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the counsel needs to repeat the Albanian references.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- you say something about the paramilitary forces, and that is they all -- they coordinated everything from the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of the Interior. Where do you get this information from, first that everything was coordinated and conducted by the Ministry of Defence and the minister of the interior, and I am going to continue with some more questions after I guess your answer to this.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I didn't get information from anyone but from the acts of the paramilitary, military, and police forces of Republic of Serbia, the action that took part in part of Trstenik area. I think it was called shoe horse -- Horseshoe operation, and from this operation I reached the conclusion that it was a coordination between the two forces. The Ministry of Defence was in charge of the army, the Ministry of the Interior was in charge of the police. To me it seemed like a single command and with -- with subordinated forces that acted under the orders of the single command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Where do you get the information, Mr. Hyseni, about the Potkovica operation, the Horseshoe operation?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I don't have direct information for this, but it is true that this plan of the military police and other forces of Serbia was called Horseshoe or Scorched Land. It is possible that I read about it in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hyseni, there is another name here, Scorched Earth. Can you please tell me if you know that operation, regardless of whether it's called Horseshoe or Scorched Earth, was a military operation or was a police operation with that name, or was it something third? I think you know the details that perhaps even I don't know, so then it would be very strange if you didn't know the answer to this.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: This was a joint coordinated operation of the whole -- of all the forces of Serbia operating in Kosova at the time. I saw this with my own eyes. I saw how people were being expelled, how areas were being ethnically cleansed, how houses were being looted. All this happened on the 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That was the time that the NATO bombing was going on as well. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes. The bombing had started, but not in Sojeve where I was. There was no bombing in Sojeve. There was no bombing of the area where the population was staying. NATO had its targets, and civilians were not one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You already talked about this and that was not my question. My next question will be you said in your village that it was a purely Albanian village with no members of other ethnic groups except Albanian, but you said that in the neighbouring villages there were Serbian families. Did these Serbian families also leave their homes?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: We're talking about Staro Selo or Fshati i Vjeter in Albanian. There were Serb or Montenegrin families living there, about 12 or 13. At that time they didn't leave the village, but they provided shelter to a very dangerous paramilitary group. I have information that this was Seselj's group, but I didn't see them myself. At the entry to the village, to this village, the police were stationed. They set on fire eight houses from some relatives of mine, and there were also people killed in the village. I've given the Prosecutor the details about these killings, and I can elaborate on that if you want. I'm talking about Staro Selo. Nine persons were killed from Staro Selo village during the bombing, two of them killed by the Black Hand. So I'm answering your question now. The Serbs did not leave their homes. They only left after the Kumanovo agreement was signed. And they set all the houses on fire as they were leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs set their houses on fire before they left Kosovo? Is that what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked to stop for the translation before he starts answering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They didn't set their own houses on fire. They burnt the Albanian houses. They are selling their houses. Their own houses are on the market. The government of Kosova has actually rebuilt their houses in some of the villages and offered them the opportunity to return, but the mere fact that they refuse to return to their homes leads one to believe that they have a hand in the ill-doings that took part during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this a convenient time, Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would not be, but, however, I do agree that we have a break. However, I will need an additional seven or eight minutes to round off this topic, but I will make a marking and remember where I left it off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good. We shall adjourn now. We have a break for half an hour. We resume at 1.00. The court officer will assist you during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, am I right in saying that your statement that the MUP and the Ministry of Defence coordinated all of the events, these are merely your assumptions, you do not have any actual facts or information to corroborate that?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: It's not an assumption if we speak about what really happened in Sojeve village. The action itself shows -- the action committed by those people part of those formations shows that they must have had a command and someone must have led them. The army has been led by the General Staff, and it is under the power of the Ministry of Defence. The police, on the other hand, was under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Interior. The paramilitary or reservists, whatever they were, they have cooperated in them, and this shows that there was a coordination. If Serbia had used a democratic form in Kosova, these things would not have happened, because the army that operated in Bibe, Strasel [phoen], Sllatine was the army from Nis, Vojna Posta Nis. This is not an assumption. I can even show you the document, the relevant document which I have submitted to the Prosecution signed by one of the captains of that army which was found in one of our homes. That's why I'm saying this is not an assumption, but it's an actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Since you mentioned documents, I'll ask you this: Did you ever see a document coordinating the work of MUP members, army members, that is to say soldiers and police, and to include the reservists or paramilitary forces, whichever way we term them. Did you ever see an order for a joint operation by soldiers, police, and reservists or paramilitaries? Did you ever come across such a document?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: A document that shows that an order has been given then is impossible for me or anyone else to see, because they are secret documents. But I'm saying the actions, the operations committed during those times, they must have been done on the basis of orders given to the army, to the police of a state or a so-called state, I would say, which Serbia -- those forces that Serbia concentrated in Kosova. These were criminal groups that did nothing other than exerted criminal violence against Albanians, civilian Albanians, elderly people, innocent people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What is the basis of your knowledge that in those operations reservists participated or -- or the paramilitaries, as you call them? What is your basis for that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: The basis of my knowledge is that the regular army, the reservists or the paramilitaries, you may call them as you like, you can distinguish them from the way they dress, from the way they act. A regular army does not wear beards. I have been a soldier myself. The uniform is in a better shape, is tidier, and is a set uniform, whereas the paramilitaries or the reservists don't have the same uniform. They are unshaven, they have long hair, and so on. On the basis of the appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was there a difference in terms of weapons carried by members of the army and members of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: It depends on the military unit involved. Mainly, the weapons were Kragujevc make weapons. Kragujevac mainly. The police had automatic rifles produced in Kragujevac. Only in one occasion I saw a soldier carrying a machine-gun, but it, too, was produced in the same place. Or in Zagreb maybe. If you're asking me about the weapons of the soldiers, an infantry platoon, when I was a soldier, and I suppose that was the case even then, don't have the same weapons. Some have submachine-guns, some have machine-guns or automatic or semi-automatic rifles. The police had usually the same weapons, Zastava make, manufactured in Kragujevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you mentioned members of an organisation called Crna Ruka, Black Hand, referring to a village in which there were a dozen Serb and Montenegrin families. First of all, how did you learn of the name of the organisation, and second of all, do you know anything more about? Do you know who those people were, what sort of clothes they wore, what weapons they had, what vehicles they used? Do you have any information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes. I have information that the Black Hand existed. The entire town knew about it. I would say the entire Kosova, because after 6.00, nobody dared go out. If anyone was caught out in the street, he would be killed. In a place called Srpski Babush, some victims were found there, and it was written on the body "Black Hand." That is, the perpetrator, who was the perpetrator. They circulated in vehicles without licence plates. They acted in concert with the police of the police station, for example. There is a policeman who was called Pucrran. I don't know his name. He was a terrible person. He used to have a BMW, and his car used to circulate always after 6.00. There were also two civilians from the town known by the name of Pesic. They also were among the perpetration. They were members of the Black Hand, but of course there were others. And these killings committed by this notorious formation were aimed at striking fear among the population and force them to flee. This became apparent, especially after the killings committed prior to the air-strikes. I am talking about Ferizaj area. And this Black Hand killed two young people in Staro Selo, Sadik Leskovci and someone from Magashi family. His name was Elhami Muharremi from the Magashi family. These two young persons were victims of this very formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that concerning the organisation Black Hand, have only indirect information and knowledge, having discussed it with various people? You do not have any direct knowledge about the organisation, do you?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: This is direct information that I have, because we dealt directly with what happened. We participated in the burial of these two young people in this case. We talked with their family members. What more direct information can you get other than this? We didn't go to the police station to ask, because if you went to the police station at that time, you were hardly likely to come out alive from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Who was the founder of this armed formation called Black Hand that you have been referring to today? What have you heard about it?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: The founder on the level of Serbia, do you mean, or for Kosova?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea whether that organisation existed in Serbia at all. You mentioned the Black Hand organisation. If you know, tell us who is the political mentor of that organisation, and share with us any -- which information you may have.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: This organisation you are asking me about, alleging that you don't know it ever existed is not correct, because it did exist. It had -- it executed people. It killed people. As to the founder of this organisation, I believe the then Serbian power must know. As for Ferizaj, I told you that some of its members were well-known faces for us. One of them to this day works in Leskovc, in the police station together with his wife. The other, I don't know where he is. As well as the state security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have in mind any political parties allegedly behind the organisation of the Black Hand?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: No. No. I have never mentioned any political party behind this Black Hand organisation. It was directly supported by the Serbian power, especially by the police, the police institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see any members of that organisation in the field where you were?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: At the time it operated, and I mentioned that it operated after 6.00 in the evening, it was impossible for me to see any one of them, because if I happened to see them, I would have been executed on the spot. My house is near the Gnjilan-Ferizaj road, and on one occasion I saw a black Golf car without licence plate, and it belonged to the Black Hand, but I couldn't see the persons inside the car, the way they were dressed, what they were carrying, from my house. I couldn't see them. I only saw the car parked at a crossing to observe if someone was coming out or moving about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that that vehicle belonged to the Black Hand? You didn't see any people. You didn't see the driver. You saw no one. You didn't see any registration plates. It's a black car standing at an intersection and yet you claim it belongs to the Black Hand organisation. Why do you think so?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I say this because nobody dared move those days. Even if you had a sick person, you wouldn't dare take him or her to the hospital. It was like a curfew. The only cars that were circulating after 6.00 were those that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can I conclude, then, that you arrived at that conclusion without any further evidence that these were members of the organisation inside the vehicle at that moment?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I am saying even now that that car belonged to the Black Hand formation, which was active during those days. I wished I would have been in a position to identify the persons inside, because many people were killed in Shati i Vjeter nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Everything you've said so far is something I believe you, but I'm asking you to tell us why you concluded that the vehicle belonged to the Black Hand organisation. You did not see the driver or anyone else. It was only your conclusion that only they could be driving in cars around at that time, but what made you conclude that that very vehicle, the black Golf car, belonged to that organisation, and if indeed that was your conclusion, I would kindly ask you to share with us the information that you based that conclusion on. Otherwise, I have to conclude that it was merely an assumption on your part.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I base this conclusion on the fact that the same Golf and other cars were observed by other members of the community there. One night, or two nights later, in another neighbourhood in the Gnjilan road, a person was wounded and was killed. They were from Viti municipality, but since I didn't see it with my own eyes I didn't testify to that. So two more victims were observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was the black Golf car seen when those people were killed?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I didn't see it myself, but this black Golf was seen that day in several other locations by various people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I have no doubts about that. The only doubt I have is concerning the person driving it and who it belonged to. Can you tell us whether you ever saw any KLA members, and I mean before you left the country for Macedonia. If you did, tell us what they looked like, whether they wore any uniforms or not, whether they had weapons and, if so, what kind of weapons?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I didn't see any KLA soldiers ever during the time you are asking me about. I only saw them on television or read about them in some newspaper article.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you see them on TV and when was it that you read those newspaper articles, before you left for Macedonia or after?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Before I left for Macedonia. We had the Bukoje [phoen] newspaper and then we watched the Albanian television via our satellite dish.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any KLA members on Albanian television?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes, but also I've seen them on CNN.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any KLA members in Urosevac and its environs, that is to say, in your village of Biba in the course of 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge that in 1988 and 1999 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that there were some KLA members in Urosevac, in your village, and other villages surrounding Biba?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: In 1998, I do have knowledge that there were KLA members there, but they were concentrated in the Nerodimlje operational zone, which is outside Ferizaj. The area where I live, Bibaj, Komogllave, Sojeve, did not have any KLA presence. There was no KLA in these villages, and the KLA was not operative in this area. It had its own positions. Had the KLA been operational in that area, these crimes perhaps wouldn't have occurred in the villages that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that members of the KLA killed, kidnapped, maltreated, raped citizens of both Serb and Albanian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: If you are talking about the Nerodimlje operational zone, I have no knowledge about that. I don't have knowledge even about other operational zones of the KLA. Personally, I think that the KLA soldiers who took the oath to defend their homeland and their people would not do such acts ever. That's why I don't think that these things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hyseni, am I right in saying that you have spent practically all your life in the village of Biba, close to Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes. Practically all my life I lived in Bibaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How well do you know your neighbours and co-villagers?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that there are people in your village who have been living there for longer than 20 years and that you don't know them?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: What do you mean by saying for longer than 20 years? You're referring to the recent 20 years? I'm not clear on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are there people who are your neighbours that you don't know, people who live in that village? I took the time period of 20 years, because there will be some questions that I plan to put that have something to do with that.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I believe, and I think I'm sure that I know all the people living in my village with the exception of some families who moved there after the war, because now things have changed. There was like a neighbourhood of Bibaj in the past which was not included in the village of Bibaj but now it's called Bibaj too. I would say I know most of the villagers living in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: The period that I was asking you about is up to 1999. Not now, but thank you for your answer. Can you please tell me the village of Trpeza. Do you know where it is?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Yes, I know where it is. It's in Viti municipality, not in Ferizaj municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Can you please tell me if you know Sadat Seljimi from Trpeza from the municipality of Vitina ?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Sir, already told you that Trpeza village is in a different municipality. I know where it is as a village, but I don't know the people from that. I knew the chief of police for Gnjilan and Ferizaj area, but I don't know this person that you mentioned by the name of Sadat Seljimi. That's why I don't know how to answer your question. To put it shortly, I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is an answer that I'm satisfied with. I don't know him. But I have to ask you, did you know - not do you know - but did you know Faruk Murselji from your village Bibaj?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Faruk who?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Murselji. Faruk Murselji?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: There is no person by the name of Faruk Murselji in Bibaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that members of the KLA carried out an attack using automatic weapons on the 9th of January, 1999 at precisely 9.00 p.m. in your village and that Mr. -- or the gentleman that you assert never lived in Bibaj, Faruk Murselji, was killed at -- in that incident, and that a person by the name of Sadat Seljimi, whom you claim that you don't know, was lightly wounded. Do you know anything about this incident or not?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I don't have any knowledge about this incident, and I doubt that it ever happened in my village. Sadat, whoever he was, is not from my village. This other person doesn't exist in my village. My village is inhabited by Albanians. That's why I don't think that your information is correct. I don't know where you got this information from, but it does not concern my area, my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You wish to say that Faruk Murselji is not an Albanian first and last name?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: It is an Albanian name, that is true, but he is not from Bibaj village, because we don't have Murselji family in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: This is why I was putting these questions to you earlier. Do you know that members of the KLA, on the 13th of March, 1999, at about 1.00 p.m. activated a powerful explosive device in front of the entrance of Jugobanka in the Catsuro Urasa [phoen] in Urosevac or Ferizaj, when Sefki Behljulji, Sefket Sulejmani were seriously wounded, and Agron Mustafu, Agron Imisti, Basri Sejdiju, Ramadus Mjaku, Sali Mehmeti and five other persons were wounded, and I don't know their names. Do you know about this event of the 13th of March in Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: No, I don't have knowledge about this incident. Could you repeat the date, please? Is it 13th of March or 13th of May? I don't think this happened in Ferizaj. At least I don't have any knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Why are you talking about the 13th of May?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: If it was 13th of May, 1999, on that day in 1999, I was in Manchester. I was a refugee. Whatever the case with the date is, I don't think this ever happened in Ferizaj. If it really happened, it would have been recorded or noted down in the Office of Human Rights and Freedoms in Ferizaj. I don't know where you got this information from.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about the 13th of March, and I have this information from reports that were published in the media, also from the MUP reports in the offices of the at that time legal sovereign state of the Republic of Serbia. Do you know that there were attacks on police officers, both Serbs and Albanians, on the territory of the entire municipality of Urosevac? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: What attacks are you talking about? Can you mention a concrete incident, a concrete period of time, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What I wanted to mention to you I have already mentioned. What I know about, I'm asking if you know about something that I don't know that relates to attacks of the KLA on citizens of Serb ethnicity and even some Albanians in the course of 1998 and 1999 in the territory of your municipality of Urosevac. Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: No. As far as the municipality of Ferizaj is concerned, I have no information about such incidents. I know that the KLA did not attack civilians. You should know that the aim of the KLA was the one to defend the population, to defend our homeland. The KLA only attacked those who generated violence, police and army. The civilians that you're mentioning, they did not attack. At least I don't have knowledge about such attacks in Ferizaj municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I were to say that members of the KLA attacked the police and the military in your area in view of what you have just said? In the transcript it says "said," but it should say "just heard," not "just said."

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: I told you that there were no attacks against civilians. However, attacks on police forces are possible. There could have been such attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement on page 4, paragraph 3 of the B/C/S, page 4, paragraph 5 of the English, and page 5, paragraph 3 of the Albanian, it says in this village, right until the beginning of the NATO bombing there were no active members of the KLA, but there was support. So in relation to that, I'm asking you, what sort of support, to whom, from whom?

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: Everybody supported it. The support came from the people. It also included financial support. It was an organisation, a formation called the Kosovo Liberation Army aimed at defending the population. Everybody supported the KLA, but not everybody could join. It was impossible for everyone to join this army. When an army is established to defend the freedom of the people, to defend their Honour, why shouldn't one support it? I am very proud of the fact that my people produced such outstanding young men who knew how to fight violence. This army wouldn't have been established had there been no violence. It was the violence exercised in all walks of life in Kosova, especially by the police, that gave rise to this army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: About the support that I asked you about, you said that you provided financial support, but I'm interested whether this means that there was also provision of food, medicines, provision of shelter, and possibly a provision of weaponry as well. Does that mean all of these things.

utterances.speaker: BEDRI HYSENI
utterances.text: No, no. Provision of shelter and weapons was impossible. As for financial support, everybody paid a percentage, a 3 per cent, when the parallel government was formed. So this financial support covered that as well. As for provision of weapons, it was impossible to have circulation of weapons everywhere. If we had such an arsenal of weapons, the 15.000 civilians that were killed in Kosova wouldn't have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, it will be a good moment to interrupt my cross-exam, and I would continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. Mr. Behar, can I ask, tomorrow after this witness is it Mr. Sterenberg who will be called?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I believe Mr. Sterenberg is our next witness, and he is ready to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And is it still the case that he must finish tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. BEHAR
utterances.text: Just a moment's indulgence. I'm being told no, that's not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Despite that, our timetable encourages us in the hope at that we can finish Mr. Sterenberg tomorrow. So if you could bear that in mind overnight, Mr. Djordjevic, when you look at your future questions for this witness and for Mr. Sterenberg. We must now adjourn for the day, Mr. Hyseni. The court staff will assist you again with the arrangements, and we continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. So we should finish your evidence not long into the morning. Thank you for that. We now adjourn until 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 22nd day of May, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
